newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Few Asian motorists to benefit from oil price drop.
newsitem.headline: Few Asian motorists to benefit from oil price drop.

text.p: Crude oil prices have slumped 20 percent this year, but few drivers in the Asia-Pacific region are going to benefit, industry sources said at the weekend.
"It does not necessarily translate into finished product," a Singapore refinery's retail manager said of the oil price drop.
Currency exchange rates, property costs and state policies are conspiring against a cut in pump prices, the sources said.
Only gas stations in New Zealand, South Korea and the Philippines cut pump prices this month. But the cuts were tiny.
New Zealanders are paying just one cent less -- NZ$0.95 (US$0.66) on average -- for a litre of gas. The price of diesel has dropped two cents.
The reason -- New Zealanders have the choice of only two grades of petrol, the higher one has special specifications and its price is actually rising.
Prices at South Korean pumps average 845-846 won ($0.96) a litre, down slightly from 848-850 won in February.
"Crude oil prices have fallen but not enough to offset the loss from the won's depreciation against the dollar," said an oil company official.
But some refiners said a few won had been snipped off the price to avoid consumer anger after a continuous rise from 815 won since price deregulation on January 1.
"We've decided to cut the price to avoid angering consumers by raising the price for three months in a row," a company official said.

In the Philippines, premium and unleaded premium gasoline prices were cut by 3.0 centavos a litre to 11.28 pesos ($0.42) and by 1.66 centavos to 10.88 pesos respectively while regular gasoline was raised by 2.33 centavos to 10.18 pesos.
Energy Regulatory Board chairman Bayani Faylona said unleaded gasoline prices were lowered in line with its policy of encouraging use of the more environmentally-friendly fuel.
Officials also attributed the cut to falling wholesale prices over the last month in Singapore, Asia's main exporter of refined products.
But in Singapore, retail prices acutally rose to a nine-month high in mid-February.
With two Singapore cents added to the price of a litre of gas, Singaporeans now pay one of the highest pump prices in the region -- US$0.83 for 98-octane unleaded gasoline.
"The price rise reflects certain costs of the finished product and overheads," said one retail manager.

He said a major concern for Singapore's six retailers, who run 246 stations in a land-scarce nation of three million people where consumption is fairly small, is the high costs of getting the land to put a gas station on.
"The latest site went for S$30 million, and that's only on a 30-year lease," he said. "Take two years off for construction... and just how much petrol can you sell in 28 years?"
Japanese motorists are also having to pay 0.5 to 0.7 yen per litre more at the pumps because the weaker yen has raised the cost of buying oil, wiping out the effect of lower U.S. dollar crude prices.

But industry analysts said they expected refiners to lower wholesale prices for April, because there is a two-month delay in passing the costs. During February, the currency market was relatively stable, they said.
"Lower wholesale prices may cause retail prices to fall," said Akira Takahashi, managing director of the Oil Information Service Centre.

But while the current oil price drop has not meant cheaper petrol in Japan, the government's loosening of its price controls two years ago has. Gas pump price wars has meant a 13-percent fall to around 106 yen ($0.86).
"Severe competition amongst gasoline stations has made it easy for prices to fall but difficult to rise," Takahashi said.

Pump prices have remained stable in other Asian-Pacific countries where the state still has some control over oil prices, such as China, India, Malaysia and Australia. (US$1.00=NZ$1.43, 878.2 won, S$1.43, 26.30 pesos, Yen 123.64)
(With contributions from Wellington, Seoul, Manila, Tokyo, Sydney, Canberra, Kuala Lumpur)
